label: Tehillim (Psalms) — Part 8 — Psalms 120–150
summary_plain: Psalms 120 through 150 include the Songs of Ascent (120-134) — pilgrim songs sung going up to Yerushalayim — and the final Halleluyah psalms. Psalm 121: I lift up my eyes to the hills — from where does my help come? My help comes from YHWH, who made heaven and earth. Psalm 127: Unless YHWH builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Psalm 137 is the exile lament: By the rivers of Babylon — there we sat down and wept when we remembered Tziyon. How shall we sing YHWH's song in a foreign land? Psalm 150 closes the entire Psalter: Let everything that has breath praise YAH. Halleluyah.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Psalms 120-150 from DSS witnesses (11QPsa, 4QPs fragments) and the Orit Ge'ez. The Songs of Ascent (Shir HaMa'alot, Psalms 120-134) are pilgrimage psalms — they accompany the physical ascent to Yerushalayim. Psalm 137 is the definitive exile psalm: 'By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept when we remembered Tziyon.' The question 'How shall we sing YHWH's song in a foreign land?' is not rhetorical — it is the central identity question of every displaced covenant community. The Beta Israel sang YHWH's songs in Ethiopia. Enslaved Africans encoded covenant memory in spirituals on plantations. The Qumran community preserved YHWH's songs in caves. Psalm 137 is the ongoing condition of every scattered Israelite community that remembers Tziyon. The 11QPsa arrangement differs significantly from the Masoretic in this section — the closing psalms appear in a different order, demonstrating that the Psalter's final shape was not fixed when the DSS were sealed.

key_terms.definition: The solar covenant calendar used by the Qumran community and preserved in the Book of Chanokh: 364 days, divided into four seasons of 91 days each (13 weeks × 4), giving exactly 52 Shabbatot per year. Every festival falls on the same day of the week every year — Shavu'ot always on the first day of the third month.

A Qumran liturgical collection (4Q400-407, 11Q17) containing 13 songs, one for each Shabbat of the first quarter of the year. Each song describes the angelic worship in the heavenly temple. The cycle mirrors the 13 Shabbatot of one quarter of the 364-day calendar.

A fixed liturgical collection sung at the three pilgrimage festivals (Pesach, Shavu'ot, Sukkot) and at Khanukkah. Egyptian Hallel (Ps.113-118) was sung before and after the Passover meal. These psalms function as the Psalter's festival liturgy.

15 psalms (Ps.120-134) each headed 'A Song of Ascents' (Shir HaMa'alot). Traditionally sung by pilgrims traveling to Yerushalayim for the three annual festivals. They form a coherent mini-collection: beginning in exile (Ps.120), arriving at Zion (Ps.122), and trusting YHWH's protection (Ps.121, 125, 127).

Psalm 81 is associated with New Moon celebration: 'Blow the trumpet at the new moon, at the full moon, on our feast day.' It calls for covenantal remembrance at the appointed time, connecting lunar calendar markers to covenant worship.

A set of Qumran calendar texts (4Q320-330) organizing the rotation of priestly courses (Mishmarot) according to the 364-day calendar. They synchronize Shabbatot, months, and festival dates with the specific priestly course serving in the Temple — connecting calendar discipline to covenant worship.

The Festival of Sukkot (Tabernacles) had the most extensive psalm liturgy: the full Egyptian Hallel was sung, and the Psalms of Ascent (Ps.120-134) were traditionally associated with the fifteen steps of the Temple and the water-drawing ceremony. Ps.118 was the great processional psalm for Sukkot.

The daily Tamid offering (morning and evening) was accompanied by specific psalm assignments: Sunday — Ps.24, Monday — Ps.48, Tuesday — Ps.82, Wednesday — Ps.94, Thursday — Ps.81, Friday — Ps.93, Shabbat — Ps.92. This calendar-psalm mapping appears in the Mishnah (Tamid 7:4) and likely reflects earlier Temple practice.

Psalm 92 is the only Shabbat-designated psalm in the Psalter: 'A Psalm, a song for the Shabbat day.' It celebrates YHWH's covenant faithfulness and the flourishing of the righteous — a weekly covenant renewal song for the day of rest that crowns the 364-day calendar cycle.

In the 364-day covenant calendar, Shavu'ot (the Festival of Weeks) always falls on the 15th of the third month — always a Sunday. This fixed date, documented in Yovelim (Book of Jubilees) and the Qumran texts, was the primary point of contention between the Qumran community and the Jerusalem Temple establishment, which used a lunar calendar that placed Shavu'ot on a shifting date.

faq.question: How does the 364-day covenant calendar connect to psalm worship?
faq.answer: The 364-day covenant calendar (preserved in Chanokh and Yovelim, and practiced at Qumran) provided an exact framework for liturgical psalm use. Because 364 = 52 × 7, every festival and Shabbat fell on the same weekday every year — Shabbat always on the seventh day, Shavu'ot always on the 15th of the third month (Sunday). This allowed fixed psalm assignments: Ps.92 always for Shabbat, Ps.24 always for Sunday Tamid, specific Hallel psalms always for the same festivals. Calendar discipline and worship were inseparable.

faq.question: What are the Psalms of Ascent and why were they sung on pilgrimage?
faq.answer: The 15 Psalms of Ascent (Shir HaMa'alot, Ps.120-134) were traditionally sung by pilgrims traveling to Yerushalayim for the three annual festivals (Pesach, Shavu'ot, Sukkot). They move from lament in exile (Ps.120) through the journey to arrival at Tzion (Ps.122) and confident covenant trust (Ps.121, 125, 127). The Hebrew word ma'alot means 'steps' or 'ascents' — both the physical ascent to the mountain city and a spiritual progression.

faq.question: What are the Egyptian Hallel psalms and when were they used?
faq.answer: The Egyptian Hallel (Ps.113-118) is a fixed liturgical collection recounting YHWH's redemption of Yisra'el from Mitzrayim (Ps.113-114) and offering praise for covenant deliverance (Ps.115-118). It was sung at the three pilgrimage festivals and at the Passover Seder — Ps.113-114 before the meal, Ps.115-118 after. Ps.118 ends: 'This is the day that YHWH has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.'

faq.question: What are the Songs of Sabbath Sacrifice and what do they reveal about Qumran worship?
faq.answer: The Songs of Sabbath Sacrifice (4Q400-407, 11Q17) are 13 liturgical songs, one for each Shabbat of the first calendar quarter. Each song describes the angelic worship in the heavenly temple — the angelic priests offering sacrifice alongside the earthly community. They reveal that the Qumran community understood their Shabbat worship as a participation in heavenly liturgy: the earthly priests and the angelic priests worshipping YHWH in synchronized covenant rhythm.

faq.question: Why was Shavu'ot's fixed date in the 364-day calendar so important?
faq.answer: In the 364-day covenant calendar, Shavu'ot always falls on the 15th of the third month (always Sunday) — the fixed covenant anniversary of the giving of Torah at Sinai. This fixed date was the central point of contention between the Qumran community and the Jerusalem Temple establishment: the Temple used a lunar calendar that placed Shavu'ot on a different, variable date. Getting this date wrong, the Qumran community believed, invalidated the entire covenant renewal ceremony — it was not a minor liturgical dispute but a question of covenant obedience.

faq.question: How were psalms assigned to the daily Tamid offering?
faq.answer: Each day of the week had a specific psalm assigned to the morning Tamid offering: Sunday — Ps.24 (YHWH's ownership of the earth), Monday — Ps.48 (YHWH's city), Tuesday — Ps.82 (divine council judgment), Wednesday — Ps.94 (YHWH as judge), Thursday — Ps.81 (covenant call with trumpet), Friday — Ps.93 (YHWH reigns), Shabbat — Ps.92 (the Shabbat song). This weekly psalm cycle embedded the entire theology of creation, covenant, justice, and worship into daily temple rhythm.

faq.question: What is Psalm 136 and why does it repeat the same phrase 26 times?
faq.answer: Psalm 136 is called the Great Hallel — 26 verses, each ending with the refrain 'for his steadfast love endures forever' (ki le'olam khasdo). The structure is antiphonal: a leader recites YHWH's acts (creation, the Exodus, the conquest), and the congregation responds with the covenant affirmation. The 26-fold repetition creates a covenant liturgy of pure steadfast-love theology: YHWH's character is the reason behind every act from creation to redemption.

faq.question: How does Psalm 24 function as the Sunday Tamid psalm?
faq.answer: Psalm 24 opens: 'The earth is YHWH's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein — for he has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers.' As the first-day Tamid psalm, it sets the week's worship foundation: everything that follows in the week's work and worship belongs to YHWH who created and owns it. The psalm then asks who may ascend YHWH's mountain — and answers with covenant moral requirements, not ritual status.

faq.question: Why is Psalm 92 specifically designated as the Shabbat psalm?
faq.answer: Psalm 92 is titled 'A Psalm, a song for the Shabbat day' — the only psalm with this designation. Its content matches: it celebrates YHWH's covenant faithfulness that is 'proclaimed in the morning and at night' (the two daily Tamid offerings), and it declares the flourishing of the righteous against the apparent prosperity of the wicked — a Shabbat meditation on the difference between the world as it appears and the covenant reality that will prevail. Shabbat rest is not idleness but covenant confidence.

faq.question: How did the Qumran community understand their calendar worship as cosmic participation?
faq.answer: The Qumran community understood the 364-day calendar as the actual structure of creation — built into the cosmos by YHWH (documented in Chanokh 72-82). Keeping the correct calendar was not a preference; it was covenant obedience. Their worship, organized by the calendar, was understood as synchronizing with the heavenly liturgy described in the Songs of Sabbath Sacrifice: the earthly priestly community and the angelic priestly community worshipping together in the same rhythm, at the same appointed times, honoring YHWH who set both the calendar and the covenant.
